Imagine someone who can only see what is right in front of their face — anything far away is a blur. They walk through life focused only on what's close, missing the bigger picture that stretches beyond.

That image is the soul of the word shortsighted. It has two meanings — one about the eyes, one about the mind — and both share this same core idea: an inability or failure to see what is far away.
Meaning 1 — The Physical Sense

In medicine and everyday speech, shortsighted describes a person whose eyes can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects clearly. A shortsighted person can read a book held in their hands but struggles to read a signboard across the street.

This is also called nearsighted (especially in American English) or myopic (the medical term).

She realized she was shortsighted when she couldn't read the blackboard from the back of the classroom.

This meaning is quite straightforward and literal.
Meaning 2 — The Figurative Sense (The More Important One)

This is the meaning you will encounter far more often in reading, writing, and conversation.

Shortsighted describes a person, decision, plan, or attitude that focuses only on the immediate present and fails to consider what will happen in the future. A shortsighted person sees only what is right in front of them — the quick, easy gain — but misses the larger, longer consequences down the road.

Just as a person with poor eyesight cannot see far into the distance, a shortsighted thinker cannot "see" far into the future.

Think of it as mental or intellectual near-sightedness.
Understanding It Deeply with Examples

Example 1:

The company made a shortsighted decision to cut its research budget to save money this year.

Here, cutting the budget saves money right now, but it means the company will produce no new products in the future, eventually hurting it badly. The decision only looked at the present and ignored the future — that's what makes it shortsighted.

Example 2:

It was shortsighted of the city government to build roads without planning for population growth.

The roads were fine for the city's current size, but no one thought about what happens in 20 years when the population doubles. By not thinking ahead, they created a future problem. That lack of forward planning is what "shortsighted" captures.

Example 3:

Eating junk food every day because it's quick and tasty is a shortsighted habit — you're ignoring what it does to your health over time.

The pleasure is immediate and clear. The damage builds slowly and is invisible in the present. Choosing short-term comfort while ignoring long-term harm is the classic pattern of shortsightedness.
The Emotion and Tone of the Word

Shortsighted is always a criticism. When you call someone or something shortsighted, you are saying it is a mistake — a failure to think properly. It carries a tone of mild disapproval or even frustration.

It suggests not necessarily that the person is unintelligent, but that they did not stop to think further ahead. It's a word about a failure of foresight, not a failure of intelligence alone.

Calling a plan shortsighted suggests the plan is flawed.
Calling a person shortsighted suggests they made a poor, hasty judgment.
Calling a policy shortsighted suggests it will cause problems in the future that its makers failed to foresee.
What Shortsightedness Looks Like in Real Life

Recognizing a shortsighted decision is easier when you ask: "Was the person or group only thinking about right now, while ignoring future consequences?"

Here are the patterns:

  • Choosing quick profit over long-term stability — a business that exploits its workers to earn more today, destroying loyalty and productivity over years.
  • Choosing convenience over consequences — cutting down forests for farmland without thinking about soil erosion and flooding a decade later.
  • Avoiding a small discomfort now at the cost of a bigger problem later — skipping a doctor's visit for a symptom that becomes a serious illness.

In every case, the shortsighted choice felt sensible or easy in the moment, but planted seeds for larger problems later.
Degrees and Variations

Shortsightedness can range from mildly poor planning to gravely irresponsible negligence. You can soften or strengthen the word with adverbs:

  • slightly shortsighted — not ideal, but understandable
  • dangerously shortsighted — seriously neglectful of important future risks
  • deeply/profoundly shortsighted — a severe failure of foresight, often used in serious contexts like politics or policy
Related Words Worth Knowing

• Farsighted — the exact opposite. A farsighted person can see far ahead and plans wisely for the future. It is the compliment to shortsighted's criticism.
  • Myopic — a formal or academic synonym for shortsighted in both its physical and figurative senses. You'll see it often in journalism and essays.
  • Narrow-minded — related in spirit, but slightly different. Narrow-minded is about being closed to other viewpoints; shortsighted is specifically about failing to think ahead in time.
  • Impulsive — acting without thinking, which often overlaps with being shortsighted, but impulsive emphasizes the speed of the decision; shortsighted emphasizes the lack of forward thinking.
A Simple Test to Know When to Use It

Ask yourself: Is this person, plan, or decision ignoring what will happen in the future in favor of what is easy, comfortable, or profitable right now?

If yes — shortsighted fits perfectly.
Summary in One Sentence

Shortsighted means either physically unable to see objects far away, or — far more commonly — describing a person, decision, or attitude that is narrowly focused on the present and fails to account for future consequences, to the point of causing later harm.
